newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan markets gyrate on banking concerns, hopes.
newsitem.headline: Japan markets gyrate on banking concerns, hopes.

text.p: Tokyo financial markets gyrated on Thursday as worries about financial sector woes jockeyed with hopes that one of the nation's most troubled banks was moving toward solving its problems.

After the close of trade, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd said its U.S. unit had posted an appraisal loss of around $50 million from derivatives deals and that the unit would suffer an after-tax loss of $83 million for 1996.

The Tokyo stock market's key barometer, the Nikkei average, tumbled to within a hair's breadth of 18,000 in late afternoon trade, as worries about Nippon Credit and rumours of losses at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi and other banks darkened sentiment.
Japanese government bond futures rose sharply on expectations that authorities would keep interest rates at current rock-bottom levels to ease bank sector pain.
A report that Nippon Credit would sell its headquarters as part of restructuring steps sent the bank's own share price tumbling by as much as nine percent.

A glimmer of optimism emerged later after report in the financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun -- later denied by the bank -- that Nippon Credit had worked out its restructuring plan including support from the central bank and a withdrawal from overseas operations.
The Nikkei average pared its lossed to close down 262.03 points, or 1.42 percent, at 18,210.42.

The newspaper report also said an expected net loss for a second consecutive year and the liquidation of bad loans would make it almost impossible for NCB to meet the capital requirements imposed on global banks.
The newspaper also said the authorities were working on ways to help support the bank's restructuring plan.

These could include use of 80 billion ($645 million) to 90 billion yen ($725 million) from a fund set up to help clean up failed mortgage firms to buy newly issued NCB shares which would then be sold to private financial institutions.
Tadao Iwaki, senior managing director of NCB, told a news conference that the bank wanted to make a decision on its restructuring plan swiftly, but that the plan was still fluid.
Iwaki also said the bank would be able to achieve an eight-percent capital adequacy ratio as of the end of March, as required for internationally operating banks.

Some market players took the reported plan as a sign of progress toward cleaning up bad loan woes. "Its restructuring would help ease worries about Japan's financial system," said one Euroyen futures trader.

But banking system worries gave the currency market the jitters, with the derivative loss talk sparking a flurry of dollar-buying during a turbulent day which saw the U.S. currency move more than one full yen on various factors.

Some industry analysts said that if Nippon Credit Bank did eventually craft a restructuring along the lines reported, the move would be positive but could place an unwelcome burden on healthier banks.

"We would view the resolution of Nippon Credit Bank positively, except for the suggestion...that the government will require some of the commercial banks to help with the costs," said Salomon Brothers Asia analyst Alicia Ogawa.
Others said the plan as reported would not be sufficient given the size of NCB's problem loans.

"If it's all true, it's disappointing because it's not enough and it's difficult to see what NCB can do on its own to get out of its bad loan problem without some form of external assistance," said Brian Waterhouse, financial analyst at HSBC James Capel Japan.
